passages.text: DYSENTERY, or BLOODY FLUX, a disease in which the patient has frequent stools, mixed with blood and slime, attended with violent gripes and a continual desire to go to stool.
It is the scourge of camps and fleets, and of crowded jails and hospitals; and it commonly rages in the end of summer and in autumn.
The causes assigned are a putrid air, the eating of unripe fruit, and a sudden stopping of the perspiration by cold and damp after great heat.
The disease is contagious; and Sir John Pringle observed, that it is chiefly spread by the privies which the sick have used, and by their foul linen.
The cure is begun with a vomit of ipecacuanha, which is reckoned almost a specific in this disease; after which the bowels are cleansed with rhubarb.
When the gripes are violent, opium is given at night to procure ease; and the patient is fed on rice, sago, and other mild and mucilaginous food.
Dysentery is a type of gastroenteritis that results in bloody diarrhea. Other symptoms may include fever, abdominal pain, and a feeling of incomplete defecation.
Dysentery is mainly caused by bacteria, most often Shigella, or by an amoeba, Entamoeba histolytica.
The infection spreads through food or water contaminated with feces, and from person to person through poor hygiene.
Through history, outbreaks of dysentery have killed large numbers of soldiers in military camps and people in crowded places.

The main treatment is to keep up fluid intake, for example with oral rehydration solution. Antibiotics are used for some bacterial cases, and amoebic dysentery is treated with drugs such as metronidazole.
Ipecacuanha root was used against dysentery from the 17th century. Its alkaloid emetine was later used to treat amoebic dysentery.
Prevention depends on hand washing, safe food and water, and good sanitation.

reasons: Both texts describe bloody stools, pain in the belly and the urge to pass stool.
Shigellosis scores well but covers only one cause.

alignments.label: Bloody stools

britannica.quote: frequent stools, mixed with blood and slime

alignments.note: Same sign. Change in language only.

alignments.label: Gripes
alignments.note: Gripes is the old word for cramping pain in the belly.

britannica.quote: a continual desire to go to stool

alignments.label: Camps and crowds

britannica.quote: It is the scourge of camps and fleets

wikipedia.quote: killed large numbers of soldiers in military camps

alignments.note: Both tie the disease to armies and crowded places.

alignments.label: Cause

britannica.quote: a putrid air, the eating of unripe fruit

alignments.note: Change in knowledge. Bacteria or an amoeba cause the disease. Bad air, fruit and stopped sweat do not.

alignments.label: Spread by the privies

britannica.quote: chiefly spread by the privies which the sick have used

wikipedia.quote: food or water contaminated with feces

alignments.note: Pringle saw that the stools of the sick carry the disease. The route through food and water was not known.

alignments.label: Ipecacuanha

britannica.quote: a vomit of ipecacuanha, which is reckoned almost a specific

wikipedia.quote: Its alkaloid emetine was later used to treat amoebic dysentery

alignments.note: The root has an effect on the amoebic form only. Inference: as a vomit it did not help the bacterial form.

alignments.label: Purging

britannica.quote: the bowels are cleansed with rhubarb

alignments.note: Change in knowledge. Treatment now replaces lost fluid. Inference: a purge adds to the loss.

alignments.label: Prevention

wikipedia.quote: Prevention depends on hand washing, safe food and water, and good sanitation

alignments.note: Wikipedia adds prevention by hygiene. The 1778 text gives none.

suggestedQuestions: How did the 1778 entry think dysentery spreads?

How did the 1778 entry think dysentery s.answer: It calls the disease contagious and, after Pringle, says it spreads chiefly by the privies the sick have used and by their foul linen [B4]. Wikipedia says it spreads through food or water contaminated with feces and through poor hygiene [W3]. The link to the stools of the sick held.

Did ipecacuanha work against dysentery?.answer: In part. The 1778 entry calls it almost a specific [B5]. Wikipedia says its alkaloid emetine was later used for amoebic dysentery [W6]. Most cases have a bacterial cause [W2], and treatment today relies on fluids and drugs such as metronidazole [W5].
